newsitem.title: USA: Balanced budget amendment may be 1st US House bill.
newsitem.headline: Balanced budget amendment may be 1st US House bill.

text.p: Supporters of a balanced budget amendment to the U.S. constitution hope it will gain the symbolic position as the first piece of legislation introduced Tuesday when the House opens for the new congressional session.

Rep. Dan Schaefer, R-Colorado, and Charles Stenholm, D-Texas, and a bipartisan group of sponsors will reintroduce the same legislation that passed the House last year 300-132 but failed in the Senate by one vote.
Negotiations are underway with House leaders to give the bill the symbolic honor of being H.R.1.

The 1996 election gave the measure another two votes in the Senate which should guarantee its passage in that chamber, but in the House supporters acknowledge they will have to work to win the necessary 290 votes. The vote is expected in early February.
A constitutional amendment must win two thirds of the House and Senate to pass and be sent to the states for ratification. It needs passage by 38 states to become law.

A spokeswoman for Schaefer said negotiations were going on with the leadership to decide whether or not the balanced budget legislation would be have the title H.R. 1. In the Senate, the amendment is expected to be one of a package of bills introduced by Senate Republicans on Jan. 21, the first legislative day in that chamber.
The distinction of being the first piece of legislation introduced is purely symbolic and while it signifies the political importance, it does not carry any preferential treatment on the House floor.
The early action is also a test case for the new bipartisanship which both Republicans and Democrats have said will characterize the two-year session.

Stephen Moore, an analyst with the private, free-market CATO Institute, noted that the amendment will be a test for possible agreement on balancing the budget. "If the balanced budget amendment passes ... that lays the groundwork for a real substantive budget agreement. If the amendment fails, I think all bets are off," he said.
